purpose: Promote only already-vetted, in-period, locally supported one-sided evidence into the canonical benchmark registry; do not manufacture two-sided labels or use observed starting population as a target.
selection_rules: The observation must describe a bounded settlement system or site with a defensible population floor.
Staple food support must be predominantly local and independently documented.
Trade, war, conquest, migration, epidemics and boundary mismatch remain explicit caveats.
Containment is sufficient for a one-sided inequality, but it is not treated as an exact historical boundary for a two-sided scale anchor.
A lower bound is never promoted to the global scale anchor and never becomes a location-level training label.

records.independence_disposition: shared_with_existing_great_zimbabwe_urban_control; not counted as a new independent source family
pressure_and_food_evidence: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Great Zimbabwe National Monument, Outstanding Universal Value, paragraphs 52-61: fourteenth-century principal city exceeded 10,000 people; farming and pastoral activity are archaeologically documented; abandonment followed food-hinterland failure near 1450.

Chirikure et al. (2017), PLOS ONE 12(6):e0178335, abstract and pp. 1-2, 9-11: the repeated 18,000-20,000 estimate is ecologically inconsistent; a 20,000 scenario requires approximately 20,000 ha arable land and 11,500-20,000 cattle, while the credible site total is unlikely to exceed 10,000.
records.trade_and_shock_review: Mixed local staple production and pastoralism with Indian Ocean prestige trade and tribute; the city boundary cannot stand for the surrounding rural catchment, so the record is a containment floor only.

mapping.historical_boundary: UNESCO Great Zimbabwe archaeological property/site, approximately 800 ha
mapping.mapping_semantics: exact containment for a one-sided inequality; not an area-equivalent historical boundary

records.decision: retain_vetted_lower_bound; no scale-anchor promotion; no regional correction factor

records.independence_disposition: independent_source family; retained as one archaeological landscape group despite multiple analyses of the same UMARP/JASP record
pressure_and_food_evidence: Earle, How Chiefs Come to Power, Table 2.2 and pp. 54-57: settlement area, occupational density and contemporaneous occupation imply approximately 61,000 Wanka II residents.
Earle pp. 56-57 and chapter 4: fortified polities competed over land, herds and resources, indicating pressure but not proving a fully saturated Malthusian ceiling.

D'Altroy, El poder provincial en el imperio inka, p. 153; Ortman et al., Settlement Scaling and Economic Change in the Central Andes, pp. 2-5 and 14-15; Costin and Earle, American Antiquity 54(4), pp. 695-701: local potato, quinoa, oca/olluco, camelid/deer, rain-fed and terraced production dominate staples; commercial markets are not the support mechanism.
records.trade_and_shock_review: Low-to-moderate staple trade; some maize and lowland specialties were exchanged. Chronic warfare and later Inka conquest are caveats; neither is converted into an anchor-specific correction.

mapping.historical_boundary: UMARP northern Upper Mantaro/Yanamarca landscape inside the approximately 1,900 km2 JASP survey region
mapping.mapping_semantics: exact containment for a one-sided inequality; selector area 11,046.64 km2 intentionally exceeds the published 1,900 km2 research landscape

records.decision: retain_vetted_lower_bound; no scale-anchor promotion; retain broad containment caveat in held-out diagnostics

summary.remaining_action: Use both only as one-sided aggregate tests; exact historical polygon reconstruction is still required before either can become a two-sided scale anchor.
